packageText: === MASTER SOURCE PACKAGE === TITLE: Temporal Bone Fractures CANONICAL HIERARCHY: All Categories > Basic > Neuroradiology > Head and Neck > Facial Trauma and Other H&N Emergencies > Temporal Bone Fractures CANONICAL DECK PATH: Corebook::Neuro::Head and Neck::Facial Trauma and Other H&N Emergencies::Temporal Bone Fractures SOURCE BASIS: [RadPrimer] canonical backbone and hierarchy; [STATdx] supplemental depth and distinct image examples. CORE STATUS: No auditable Core Radiology source pages were provided in this bundle. Do not generate Core-specific claims from this package alone. === SOURCE SYNTHESIS NOTES === [Both] RadPrimer and STATdx share the core article text for temporal bone fractures. RadPrimer is retained as the canonical hierarchy/backbone because metadata.json canonicalHierarchy must be used exactly for routing. [RadPrimer] The backbone emphasizes bone-algorithm MDCT with coronal reconstructions; CTA/MRA when carotid canal injury is suspected; CTV/MRV when a dural venous sinus or jugular foramen region is involved; and dedicated brain imaging because intracranial injuries are common. [STATdx] STATdx contributes distinct additional images beyond the RadPrimer set, especially ossicular dislocation/fracture, pneumolabyrinth, carotid injury, pseudofracture mimics, MR correlation, chronic labyrinthitis ossificans, and posttraumatic cephalocele. [Both] STATdx fully covers the RadPrimer image set: STATdx images 1-10 are exact duplicate copies of RadPrimer images 1-10 by stable image ID and visual evidence review. RadPrimer copies remain primary because RadPrimer is the canonical source. === DIFFERENTIAL DIAGNOSIS BACKBONE === [Both] - Pseudofractures: sutures, fissures, canaliculi, and aqueducts. Favor a pseudofracture when the lucency is bilateral/symmetric and has smooth corticated margins. - Incus interposition procedure: surgical remodeling/realignment of the incus can mimic chronic incus dislocation. - Mastoiditis or mastoid/middle-ear effusion: preexisting opacification may not represent acute hemotympanum or CSF leak. === ESSENTIAL TEACHING POINTS === [Both] Classify temporal bone fractures by otic capsule status because otic-capsule-violating fractures better predict sensorineural hearing loss, facial nerve injury, and CSF leak than the older longitudinal/transverse system. [Both] Longitudinal fractures parallel the petrous ridge long axis and commonly involve the external auditory canal, middle ear, and ossicles while usually sparing the otic capsule. [Both] Transverse fractures are perpendicular to the petrous ridge long axis and more often involve the otic capsule and facial nerve, with less frequent external auditory canal or middle-ear involvement. [Both] Many fractures are oblique or mixed, so report both the anatomic orientation and whether the otic capsule is violated. [Both] Secondary signs include hemotympanum, pneumolabyrinth, and intracranial or extracranial air/hemorrhage near the mastoid. Unexplained parapharyngeal space air should prompt a search for mastoid fracture. [Both] Ossicular dislocations are more common than ossicular fractures; incudostapedial disruption is most common, followed by incudomalleolar disruption and complete incus dislocation. [Both] The most clinically important structures to assess are the facial nerve canal, otic capsule, tegmen, carotid canal, and ossicles; also evaluate intracranial contents and cervical spine injuries. [Both] Consider CTA/MRA if the fracture reaches the carotid canal, and CTV/MRV if the fracture reaches the dural venous sinus or jugular foramen region. [Both] MR can help assess hemolabyrinth, facial nerve or membranous labyrinth enhancement, subacute intracranial complications, ICA injury, venous thrombosis, and suspected posttraumatic labyrinthitis ossificans. === CLINICAL AND MANAGEMENT POINTS === [Both] Common clinical findings include Battle sign, external auditory canal hemorrhage, hemotympanum, conductive hearing loss, sensorineural hearing loss, facial nerve dysfunction, CSF leak, and vertigo. [Both] Conductive hearing loss initially may reflect hemotympanum or tympanic membrane injury; persistent conductive loss should prompt careful ossicular evaluation. [Both] Immediate complete facial paralysis has a worse recovery prognosis than delayed paresis; delayed paresis often reflects reversible injury and is commonly observed, sometimes with steroids. [Both] Most CSF leaks resolve spontaneously within 7 days, but persistent leaks may require surgery. Meningitis can occur in a minority of patients with CSF leak. [Both] Severe head injury management takes priority. Carotid injury may require anticoagulation and/or endovascular therapy. Antibiotics are used when CSF leak is present. === PRIMARY IMAGE SET FOR FUTURE GENERATION === [RadPrimer] RadPrimer image 1: Axial NECT of the right temporal bone in a 37-year-old man who was assaulted shows a longitudinal fracture plane causing subtle widening of the incudostapedial joint and propagating through the anterior wall of the epitympanum . [RadPrimer] RadPrimer image 2: Axial NECT in the same patient shows an inferior continuation of the longitudinal fracture through the posterior wall of the TMJ fossa and eustachian tube , and questionably into the carotid canal . A follow-up CTA was negative for carotid injury. [RadPrimer] RadPrimer image 3: Composite mirrored axial NECTs in a 34-year-old man show an otic capsule violating (OCV) fracture that traverses the posterior semicircular canal (SCC) as well as the anterior and posterior limbs of lateral SCC. Normal anatomy is visible in the right-hand panel. [RadPrimer] RadPrimer image 4: Axial NECT in a 57-year-old man who inserted a cotton swab through the tympanic membrane shows disruption of the incudostapedial joint . There is also a fragment of the otic capsule displaced medially into the tympanic facial nerve canal . [RadPrimer] RadPrimer image 5: Axial NECT in a 73-year-old man with trauma shows a transverse OCV fracture plane extending through the vestibule. The fracture reaches the tympanic segment of the facial nerve more anteriorly. [RadPrimer] RadPrimer image 6: Axial NECT in the same patient shows the fracture plane reaching the round window niche . More anteriorly, the fracture is extending through the lateral aspect of the basal turn of the cochlea to the anterior aspect of the otic capsule. [RadPrimer] RadPrimer image 7: Sagittal CT in a 47-year-old man with trauma shows a fracture involving anterior and posterior walls of the external auditory canal. There is a more posterior component of the fracture breaching the tegmen mastoideum . [RadPrimer] RadPrimer image 8: Composite mirrored sagittal images of the right and left temporal bones in the same patient show extension of a fracture plane through the right facial nerve genu and tegmen tympani in the left-hand panel. The normal left facial nerve genu is visible for comparison in the right-hand panel. [RadPrimer] RadPrimer image 9: Axial FLAIR MR in the same patient shows an acute subdural hematoma , subarachnoid hemorrhage , and a hemorrhagic contusion of the inferomedial frontal lobe. [RadPrimer] RadPrimer image 10: Coronal T1 C+ FS MR in the same patient shows abnormal signal in the superior internal auditory canal . Considering the fracture through the genu seen on CT, this signal may represent T1-intense blood products, reactive enhancement, or both. There is reactive dural enhancement along the periphery of the right temporal lobe . [STATdx] STATdx image 11: Axial bone CT shows bilateral otic capsule-sparing fractures and left malleoincudal dislocation . [STATdx] STATdx image 12: Axial bone CT shows a transverse fracture crossing the internal auditory canal and otic capsule . Note a tiny air bubble (pneumolabyrinth) in the cochlea. [STATdx] STATdx image 13: Axial bone CT reveals a longitudinal otic capsule-violating fracture extending from mastoid to petrous apex. Malleoincudal disruption is noted. Middle ear debris (hemotympanum) is present. [STATdx] STATdx image 14: Axial bone CT shows a transverse fracture extending through the fundus of the internal auditory canal associated with acute complete hearing loss due to cochlear nerve transection. [STATdx] STATdx image 15: Axial bone CT reveals a transverse OCV fracture extending from the posterior petrous surface to the vestibule . Note middle ear fluid from a perilymphatic fistula. [STATdx] STATdx image 16: Axial bone CT demonstrates complete incus dislocation with an incus fragment lodged within the external auditory canal . Tympanic membrane rupture was also present. [STATdx] STATdx image 17: Axial bone CT reveals abnormal widening of malleoincudal articulation , consistent with traumatic dislocation. The patient was imaged because of persistent conductive hearing loss after head trauma. [STATdx] STATdx image 18: Axial CTA demonstrates lack of enhancement in the left distal internal carotid artery secondary to posttraumatic occlusion in a teenager with bilateral complicated temporal bone fractures (not shown) and involvement of the carotid canal . [STATdx] STATdx image 19: Coronal bone CT shows a lucency at the junction of the long and lenticular processes of the incus . Persistent conductive hearing loss should prompt a careful search for ossicular injury; this subtle fracture was confirmed at surgery. [STATdx] STATdx image 20: Axial bone CT in a 16-year-old patient following a fall from a truck demonstrates a nondepressed, otic capsule-sparing longitudinal temporal bone fracture . [STATdx] STATdx image 21: Axial bone CT in the same patient shows the posterior aspect of the longitudinal fracture and subtle medial subluxation of the malleus head seen as the "ice cream" sliding off of the "cone," consistent with ossicular dislocation. [STATdx] STATdx image 22: Axial bone CT in a 14-year-old patient following a severe head injury shows a medial transverse, OCV fracture traversing the vestibule with extension into the medial aspect of the tympanic facial nerve canal . [STATdx] STATdx image 23: Axial bone CT more inferiorly in the same patient shows the typical inferior extension of the fracture across the jugular foramen into the round window niche . [STATdx] STATdx image 24: Axial bone CT reveals a transverse OCV fracture extending through the labyrinthine CNVII canal and the vestibule . This medial subtype of transverse fracture often results in complete and permanent sensorineural hearing loss and facial palsy. [STATdx] STATdx image 25: Axial bone CT shows a chronic transverse fracture line extending through the otic capsule to the basal turn of the cochlea , where abnormal high density in the basal turn indicates the presence of labyrinthitis ossificans. [STATdx] STATdx image 26: Axial bone CT in the same child shows a subtle longitudinal fracture involving the lateral mastoid cortex , subtle widening of the incudomalleolar joint , and air in the vestibule and cochlea . [STATdx] STATdx image 27: Coronal bone CT demonstrates a large traumatic defect of the tegmen tympani with herniation of soft tissue into the epitympanum, representing a small acquired cephalocele. The most common complication of a tegmen fracture is transient CSF otorrhea. [STATdx] STATdx image 28: Coronal bone CT reveals pneumolabyrinth . Linear lucency through the otic capsule was initially diagnosed as a fracture but represents the normal singular canal . Comparison with the contralateral temporal bone will help exclude pseudofractures. [STATdx] STATdx image 29: Axial bone CT shows a longitudinal otic-capsule-sparing fracture extending to the tegmen tympani ; thus, this patient is at risk for a CSF leak. There is widening of the incudomalleolar joint , the most common form of ossicular disruption. [STATdx] STATdx image 30: Axial bone CT demonstrate a typical transverse, OCV temporal bone fracture extending through the fundus of the internal auditory canal and base of the vestibule. The middle ear fluid could be blood or perilymph. [STATdx] STATdx image 31: Axial bone CT shows a typical malleal-incudal posttraumatic dislocation as disruption of the normal "ice cream on a cone" relationship between the head of the malleus ("ice cream") and short process of the incus ("cone"). Opacification of the posterior middle ear and mastoid antrum is secondary to resolving blood products. [STATdx] STATdx image 32: Axial temporal bone CT shows a longitudinal temporal bone fracture traversing the mastoid air cells and middle ear cavity with violation of the otic capsule. The fracture extends to the oval window with air seen in the vestibule (pneumolabyrinth). The diffuse middle ear and mastoid debris is likely both blood and CSF. [STATdx] STATdx image 33: Axial bone CT shows an unusual longitudinal OCV fracture with medial subluxation of the malleus head . The fracture extends to the oval window with pneumolabyrinth ; these findings may indicate the presence of perilymph fistula. There is medial extension to the internal auditory canal . [STATdx] STATdx image 34: Axial NECT shows complete incus dislocation. The incus is laterally displaced into the external auditory canal and rotated into the horizontal plane. Its articulations with the malleus and stapes are disrupted. [STATdx] STATdx image 35: Axial bone CT demonstrates a transverse fracture that extends to the jugular bulb and round window niche . Stapediovestibular joint disruption is suggested by the alignment of the anterior stapedial crus with the posterior margin of the oval window . [STATdx] STATdx image 36: Axial bone CT reveals a chronic fracture with medial extension to the fundus of the internal auditory canal . The CNVII canal is involved in the midtympanic segment , and the incudomalleolar joint is grossly widened . [STATdx] STATdx image 37: Axial bone CT demonstrates linear lucency through the anterior wall of the external auditory canal, representing the normal tympanosquamous fissure ; this was initially misdiagnosed as a fracture. A true fracture line extends through the anterior aspect of the glenoid fossa . [STATdx] STATdx image 38: Oblique reformatted bone CT ~ 45⁰ in the sagittal/coronal plane in a 58-year-old man status post motor vehicle accident is shown. The image is parallel to the petrous ridge long axis, perpendicular to a transverse fracture, which was seen on axial images (not shown). The fracture extends through the facial nerve genu . [STATdx] STATdx image 39: Axial bone CT in the same patient, slightly more superior than the preceding image, shows the fracture plane extending into the posteromedial aspect of the vestibule . There is associated near complete opacification of the middle ear cavity and mastoid air cells. [STATdx] STATdx image 40: Axial bone CT in a 25-year-old woman status post fall shows a capsule-sparing longitudinal fracture in the mastoid complex and widening of the incudomallear joint , consistent with ossicular disruption. [STATdx] STATdx image 41: Sagittal bone CT reformation in the same patient depicts separation of the malleus and incus . Disruption of the tegmen tympani is also visible. The fracture plane also breaches the external auditory canal into the TMJ . [STATdx] STATdx image 42: Coronal bone CT in a 73-year-old man with right-sided hearing loss and a history of trauma 1 month earlier shows a vertically oriented fracture involving the lateral SCC. [STATdx] STATdx image 43: Axial bone CT in a 1-year-old child status post fall from a chair onto a tile floor demonstrates a subtle longitudinal fracture along the anterior margin of the mastoid air cells with associated pneumolabyrinth in the vestibule. [STATdx] STATdx image 44: Axial CISS MR in the same patient demonstrates loss of the normal hyperintense T2 signal in the right lateral SCC , which can indicate hemolabyrinth or posttraumatic labyrinthitis ossificans. Notice normal T2 hyperintensity in the left lateral SCC . [STATdx] STATdx image 45: Oblique bone window reformation ~ 45° in sagittal/coronal planes in a 58-year-old man with trauma shows separation of the malleoincudal joint and malrotation of the malleus and incus. [STATdx] STATdx image 46: Coronal bone CT in a 15-year-old patient who suffered a longitudinal otic capsule-sparing temporal bone fracture 8 years ago demonstrates a large tegmen tympani defect at the site of the original fracture plane and middle ear opacification, concerning for cephalocele. Note the ossicle displacement laterally . [STATdx] STATdx image 47: Coronal T2WI FSE MR in the same patient confirms herniation of the inferior right temporal lobe through the tegmen tympani defect, consistent with posttraumatic cephalocele. [STATdx] STATdx image 48: Axial bone CT in a 42-year-old man status post trauma from a motor vehicle accident shows an OCV medial transverse fracture through the posterior aspect of the petrous ridge, extending to the basal turn of the cochlea . === IMAGE COVERAGE GATE === [Both] STATdx fully covers the RadPrimer image set. Exact duplicate pairs: RadPrimer image 1 = STATdx image 1; RadPrimer image 2 = STATdx image 2; RadPrimer image 3 = STATdx image 3; RadPrimer image 4 = STATdx image 4; RadPrimer image 5 = STATdx image 5; RadPrimer image 6 = STATdx image 6; RadPrimer image 7 = STATdx image 7; RadPrimer image 8 = STATdx image 8; RadPrimer image 9 = STATdx image 9; RadPrimer image 10 = STATdx image 10. [RadPrimer] RadPrimer images 1-10 remain the canonical primary set and preserve the RadPrimer hierarchy/backbone. [STATdx] STATdx images 1-10 are archive-optional exact duplicate copies. STATdx images 11-48 are visually distinct supplemental recognition examples and remain selected primary images. === GENERATOR ROUTING INSTRUCTIONS === Use the canonicalHierarchy exactly as: ["All Categories", "Basic", "Neuroradiology", "Head and Neck", "Facial Trauma and Other H&N Emergencies", "Temporal Bone Fractures"]. Use the deck path exactly as: Corebook::Neuro::Head and Neck::Facial Trauma and Other H&N Emergencies::Temporal Bone Fractures. Use human-facing labels such as RadPrimer image 5 and STATdx image 38 in narrative prose. Keep short IDs such as RP-05 and SDX-38 for registry, filenames, manifest, and traceability fields. Download only selectedPrimaryImageIds by default. ArchiveOptionalImageIds are exact duplicate/recovery copies and should not drive routine cards or lecture. Do not create cards or lecture content from this package yet.

sourceSelectionPlan.textBackbone: Use RadPrimer as the canonical hierarchy and differential backbone. The STATdx article text substantially overlaps the RadPrimer source; keep RadPrimer ordering and add STATdx mainly for supplemental image depth and image-specific complications.
keepFromRadPrimer: Canonical hierarchy and deck routing from metadata.json canonicalHierarchy/canonicalDeckPath.
Core classification backbone: otic-capsule-violating versus otic-capsule-sparing, and longitudinal/transverse/oblique orientation as a secondary descriptor.
Systematic search pattern: CNVII canal, otic capsule, tegmen, carotid canal, ossicles, intracranial contents, and cervical spine injuries.
RadPrimer images 1-10 as the canonical primary image set and primary same-patient clusters.
keepFromSTATdx: STATdx images 11-48 as distinct supplemental recognition examples covering additional OCS/OCV patterns, ossicular injuries, carotid injury, pseudofracture pitfalls, MR correlation, chronic complications, and cephalocele.
Source-qualified captions and URLs for all retained STATdx supplemental images.
No replacement of RadPrimer hierarchy or deck path.
downweightOrSkip: Do not use STATdx breadcrumb for routing.
